|US–China strategic stability doesn’t reach the water
US–China strategic stability doesn’t reach the water
Nearly six months after Xi Jinping and Donald Trump agreed in Beijing to build a “constructive” relationship of strategic stability (Opens in new window), a formula they reaffirmed at the White House in September (Opens in new window), their militaries are talking again. Yet in the last week of October, Chinese navy and coast guard ships were active from Japan’s southern straits to the waters off Mindanao.
These facts are not a contradiction. The framework never promised to freeze military competition, and judged against its actual commitments it is making modest progress. The problem is narrower and more serious: the channels that exist do not fit together where dangerous encounters can occur. Whatever the intent, the effect is that bilateral calm and regional pressure coexist.
Start with what was promised. According to Beijing’s summit readout, the two militaries agreed to conclude a memorandum (Opens in new window) on crisis communication and prevention “as soon as possible”. The White House fact sheet did not mention it (Opens in new window), and a US official reportedly said (Opens in new window) the subject was not discussed. Command-level contact has nonetheless resumed: the US Indo-Pacific commander met his Chinese counterpart (Opens in new window) responsible for the Taiwan Strait in Canada.
PLA air activity around Taiwan was still below last year’s level in September. The Taiwan Security Monitor counted 255 sorties in September, 43% fewer than in September 2025 (Opens in new window), although activity rebounded from August. Maritime pressure presents a different picture: on 31 October, Beijing announced coast guard patrols east of Taiwan (Opens in new window), which Taipei challenged. The lower sortie count, therefore, offers an incomplete measure of restraint.
The calendar now matters.
The strongest defence of the framework is that crisis management allows rivals to maintain deterrence while preventing accidents from escalating. US Army Pacific still treats 2027 as a readiness benchmark (Opens in new window), although news agency Reuters reported on 1 October, citing unnamed sources, that US officials considered a military operation before 2028 increasingly unlikely (Opens in new window). Pressure below the threshold of war nevertheless continues. On 23 October, Taiwan’s coast guard warned that coordinated Chinese militia and coast guard operations (Opens in new window) were increasing pressure on Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines.
The harder problem is scope. On 27 October, three Chinese warships and a coast guard ship passed together through Japan’s Osumi Strait, the first time Japan’s defence ministry has disclosed (Opens in new window) the two services travelling together through Japanese waters. Further south, the Liaoning carrier group sailed around the Philippines and did not answer Philippine radio challenges (Opens in new window), although Manila said there was no cause for alarm (Opens in new window). By 28 October, Taipei counted 53 Chinese vessels, 34 of them warships (Opens in new window), between southern Japan and the Philippines.
The Liaoning ran a similar loop (Opens in new window) in October 2024. Ship movements alone do not prove coercion. But the US intelligence community did expect Chinese pressure on Japan to intensify (Opens in new window) through 2026, while US–China channels do not directly connect the vessels involved.
A 2024 exercise between the US Coast Guard and Philippine Coast Guard (Elijah Murphy/DVIDS)
Regional channels do exist. Japan and China opened a defence hotline in 2023 (Opens in new window), and Manila and Beijing agreed in 2024 (Opens in new window) to improve maritime communications, including a future coast guard link. In August, The Interpreter reported that the Japan–China hotline had barely been used (Opens in new window) since its first call in May 2023. Manila said in March that amendments to its coast guard agreement were under discussion (Opens in new window). The gap is not an absence of channels but their coverage, reliability and coordination. A US–China memorandum alone cannot establish procedures for Chinese coast guard captains and Philippine or Japanese commanders when their ships meet.
Two further gaps compound the problem. The first is meaning. Xi has defined stability as including competition within proper limits (Opens in new window), and within days of the summit Beijing’s foreign ministry invoked the leaders’ consensus on Taiwan (Opens in new window). A US military official described Washington’s aim as enabling “both strategic stability and deterrence by denial (Opens in new window)”. Washington views allied exercises as credible deterrence; Beijing can portray them as breaching that consensus.
The second is implementation. Nuclear risk offers another test. US and Chinese officials met at least three times this year (Opens in new window) on the margins of the five nuclear powers’ dialogue, with Washington seeking more advance notice of missile tests. The reported meetings establish engagement, but not a shared launch-notification procedure.
The calendar now matters. Trump is expected in Shenzhen (Opens in new window) for APEC on 18–19 November, and Xi in Miami for the G20 on 14–15 December (Opens in new window).
Two indicators deserve attention. The first is operational: whether both governments agree on the memorandum’s purpose and scope, sign it, and use its procedures when an interception goes wrong. The second is whether the PLA’s November–December peak drill season (Opens in new window) passes without a large exercise around Taiwan. Neither would prove the framework caused restraint, but together they would suggest stability is becoming practice rather than language.
The region should also look beyond the bilateral line. Incidents involving coast guards and allies can also escalate. Extending rules for unplanned encounters to coast guards, and linking allied, regional and US–China channels, would do more for stability than another summit communiqué. Without that, the formula will have stabilised the conversation, not the competition. High-level stabilisation will remain incomplete where maritime incidents are most likely to occur.
Dr Sophie Wushuang Yi is a Postdoctoral Teaching Fellow at Schwarzman College, Tsinghua University. She is also a Non-Resident Research Fellow at the Grandview Institution in Beijing and the Wang Gungwu Visiting Fellow at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore.

乌克兰计划用自己的无人机取代中国大疆无人机
乌克兰计划用自己的无人机取代中国大疆无人机
修改日期: 2026 年 11 月 13 日
一架乌克兰侦察无人机正在接受 BRAVE1 和乌克兰国防部的测试，这是部署国产大疆 Mavic 无人机替代品的努力的一部分。
一架乌克兰侦察无人机正在接受 BRAVE1 和乌克兰国防部的测试，这是部署国产大疆 Mavic 无人机替代品的努力的一部分。
乌克兰的 Brave1 集群和国防部测试了九家乌克兰制造商的 Mavic 型侦察无人机，其中最好的正在转向采购。
Brave1 表示，替代品必须能够抵抗干扰、在没有 GPS 的情况下飞行并在空中停留至少 60 分钟。
在测试了九家乌克兰制造商的型号后，乌克兰正着手购买国产侦察无人机，以取代 Mavic，这是乌克兰军队自战争开始以来一直依赖的小型中国制造的四轴飞行器。
政府支持的国防技术集群 Brave1 周四在社交媒体上表示，它与乌克兰国防部一起进行了测试。声明称，“在测试场上证明有效并满足军事要求的无人机现在正在进入采购阶段”。其他制造商获得了详细的反馈来改进他们的设计。
Brave1 没有透露这些公司的名称，也没有透露这九家公司中有多少家通过了，也没有给出即将签订的合同的规模或价值。
- 广告 - 继续阅读下面 -
Mavic由中国大疆创新制造，是一款专为航空摄影而设计的折叠消费级无人机。乌克兰和俄罗斯军队多年来一直驾驶它来发现目标并监视前线。
“Mavic 已成为战术级侦察的关键工具，”Brave1 写道。 “但战争不断提高对无人机的要求。”
该集群表示，随着双方无人机监视的地面范围越来越宽，部队需要能够飞得更远、航程更远并在俄罗斯干扰下继续工作的飞机。 “民用无人机越来越无法满足这些要求，”它补充道。
Brave1列出了乌克兰替代者必须做的四件事。它必须能够抵抗电子战，并且在没有GPS的情况下飞行，在空中停留至少60分钟，并让操作员在更安全的距离进行控制。它还需要士兵已经知道的界面，这样部队就不必重新训练。
该集群表示：“因此，我们的目标不是复制“Mavic”，而是打造一款“适应现代战争现实”的乌克兰无人机。
- 广告 - 继续阅读下面 -
乌克兰已经为此努力了一段时间。 2024 年 11 月，八家乌克兰 Mavic 型无人机制造商为军方和政府官员执行了长达 10 公里（6 英里）的测试任务，其中两架已获准用于军事用途。
Brave1 现在与 2,500 多家乌克兰国防公司建立了联系。据国防部称，军队已收到通过其在线市场订购的 774,000 架无人机和其他物品，价值 11.5 亿美元。
Brave1 表示，它希望乌克兰无人机“能够快速适应战场变化，并且能够扩大规模”。

Ukraine moves to replace Chinese DJI drones with its own
Ukraine moves to replace Chinese DJI drones with its own
Modified date: Nov 13, 2026
A Ukrainian reconnaissance drone undergoes testing by BRAVE1 and Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence as part of efforts to field domestically produced alternatives to DJI Mavic drones.
A Ukrainian reconnaissance drone undergoes testing by BRAVE1 and Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence as part of efforts to field domestically produced alternatives to DJI Mavic drones.
Ukraine's Brave1 cluster and Defense Ministry tested Mavic-style reconnaissance drones from nine Ukrainian manufacturers, and the best are moving to procurement.
Brave1 says a replacement must resist jamming, fly without GPS and stay airborne for at least 60 minutes.
Ukraine is moving to buy homegrown reconnaissance drones to replace the Mavic, the small Chinese-made quadcopter its troops have relied on since the start of the war, after testing models from nine Ukrainian manufacturers.
Brave1, the government-backed defense technology cluster, said on social media on Thursday that it ran the tests with Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence. Drones “that proved effective on the testing ground and met military requirements are now advancing to the procurement stage,” it said. The other manufacturers got detailed feedback to improve their designs.
Brave1 didn’t name the companies, say how many of the nine passed, or give a size or value for the coming contracts.
- ADVERTISEMENT - CONTINUE READING BELOW -
The Mavic, made by China’s DJI, is a folding consumer drone built for aerial photography. Both Ukrainian and Russian troops have flown it for years to spot targets and watch the front line.
“The Mavic has become a key tool for tactical-level reconnaissance,” Brave1 wrote. “But the war is constantly raising the requirements for UAVs.”
As the band of ground watched by drones on both sides grows wider, the cluster said, units need aircraft that can fly longer, reach farther and keep working under Russian jamming. “Civilian drones are increasingly unable to meet these requirements,” it added.
Brave1 listed four things a Ukrainian replacement must do. It has to resist electronic warfare and fly without GPS, stay in the air for at least 60 minutes, and let operators control it from a safer distance. It also needs an interface soldiers already know, so units don’t have to retrain.
“The goal, therefore, is not to create a copy of the Mavic,” the cluster said, but to build a Ukrainian drone “adapted to the realities of modern warfare.”
- ADVERTISEMENT - CONTINUE READING BELOW -
Ukraine has been working on this for a while. In November 2024, eight Ukrainian makers of Mavic-style drones flew test missions of up to 10 km (6 miles) for military and government officials, and two of them had already been approved for military use.
Brave1 now links more than 2,500 Ukrainian defense companies. Military units have received 774,000 drones and other items ordered through its online marketplace, worth $1.15 billion, according to the Ministry of Defence.
Brave1 said it wants Ukrainian drones that “can quickly adapt to changes on the battlefield and can be scaled up.”

布兰奇在新闻发布会上表示，“当然”联邦调查局正在调查有关爱丽丝·黄为中国政府工作的报道。
美国总统唐纳德·特朗普在周四晚些时候发布的采访中被问及黄是否应该辞职时，重申尚未确定爱丽丝·黄是否是间谍。

“最重要的是，这名女子是间谍吗？我不知道这是否已经确定。但如果这名女子是间谍，是的。如果这名女子不是间谍，也许情况会有所不同，”特朗普告诉“直截了当的射手”播客，并补充说他周三与黄仁勋进行了交谈。
黄仁勋于周四辞职，这场离职事件持续了一年多，始于 2025 年 10 月《纽约时报》的一篇报道，将他与总部位于新加坡的 Megaspeed 前高管 Alice Huang 联系起来，Megaspeed 是 Nvidia 的官方云合作伙伴，这一令人垂涎的地位使其能够优先获得 Nvidia 芯片。
在这张由 TVBS 提供的视频中拍摄的图片中，2025 年 5 月 22 日，爱丽丝·黄 (Alice Huang) 参加了 Nvidia 首席执行官黄仁勋 (Jensen Huang) 在台湾台北一家餐厅举办的晚宴。照片通过美联社分发
随后的报道称，美国情报官员认为爱丽丝·黄代表中国情报部门行事。北京否认黄爱丽是间谍。记者未能联系到爱丽丝·黄置评。
新加坡内政部周四表示，黄爱丽丝于二月份离开新加坡，在对可能的罪行进行调查后，她被禁止再次入境。该部表示，调查与间谍活动无关。
11月8日，黄仁勋承认他对妻子不忠，但没有提供具体的关系细节。

U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said ​on Thursday that the Justice Department has not yet reached a ‌conclusion on whether Alice Huang, the Chinese businesswoman who had an affair with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, was a Chinese spy.
Blanche said at a press conference that "of course" the FBI was investigating reports that Alice Huang was working for the Chinese government.
U.S. President Donald Trump, asked in an interview released ⁠later on Thursday whether Huang should have resigned, reiterated that it was not yet determined whether Alice Huang was a spy.
U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche speaks at a news conference in Washington on Nov. 12, 2026. Photo by AP
"The big thing is, was the woman a spy? And I don't know if that's been determined yet. But if the woman was a spy, yes. If the woman was not a spy, perhaps it would be different," Trump told the "Straight Shooter" podcast, adding that he spoke to Jensen Huang on Wednesday.
Jensen Huang stepped down on Thursday in a departure that ‌unfolded ⁠over more than a year, beginning with an October 2025 New York Times report linking him to Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, an official Nvidia cloud partner, a coveted status that gave it priority access to Nvidia chips.
In this image taken from video provided by TVBS, Alice Huang attends a dinner hosted by Jensen Huang, Nvidia's CEO, at a restaurant in Taipei, Taiwan, May 22, 2025. Photo handed out via AP
Subsequent reports said U.S. intelligence ⁠officials believed Alice Huang was acting on behalf of Chinese intelligence. Beijing has denied Alice Huang is a spy. Alice Huang could not be reached for comment.
Alice Huang left Singapore ⁠in February and was barred from re-entering after an investigation into possible offences, the country's Home Affairs Ministry said on Thursday. The ministry said the investigation did ⁠not concern espionage.
On Nov. 8, Jensen Huang admitted he was unfaithful to his wife without providing details about the relationship.

BEIJING, Nov 13 - China is willing to expand cooperation with South Korea in traditional and emerging sectors including artificial intelligence and biomedicine, Foreign Minister Wang Yi said on Friday.
• In a meeting with his South Korean counterpart Cho Hyun, Wang said the two countries are "close neighbours that cannot be moved away" and "maintaining good-neighbourliness and friendship is the right choice for both sides," according to a statement released by China's Foreign Ministry
• The South Korean diplomat is on a two-day visit to China starting Friday
• China-South Korea relations were "back onto the right track" after their leaders' exchanges since late last year, Wang said
• Ties soured under Yoon Suk Yeol, the predecessor of South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, who drew Seoul closer to Washington and Tokyo
• Lee, who took office in June 2025, has sought to restore relations, hosting Chinese President Xi Jinping in Gyeongju in late 2025 and making a state visit to China in January
• China is willing to further enhance mutual trust with South Korea and expand their common interests, Wang said
• Next week, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung will visit China and attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders' meeting in Shenzhen REUTERS

content:
黄仁勋的倒台会削弱中国的人工智能雄心吗？ |海峡时报
黄仁勋的倒台会削弱中国的人工智能雄心吗？
立即注册：深入了解亚洲的快速发展
英伟达前首席执行官黄仁勋五月份在北京向媒体发表讲话，他因成为外国情报机构的目标而受到调查。
Published Nov 13, 2026, 10:05 PM
Updated Nov 13, 2026, 10:05 PM
黄仁勋在英伟达的辞职引发了人们的担忧，即美国可能会收紧芯片控制，威胁中国获得先进人工智能计算的机会。
中国称这些间谍指控“毫无根据”，并表示美国正在利用这些指控作为对中国“技术封锁”的借口。
分析师表示，短期内中国人工智能企业面临的压力可能会增加，但这种冲击也可能会加速国内芯片的发展。
北京 — — 英伟达首席执行官黄仁勋突然辞职引发了有关中国获取美国先进人工智能芯片的新问题，北京指责华盛顿利用间谍指控为更严格的技术限制辩护，尽管中国分析人士淡化了潜在影响。
黄仁勋曾亲自游说美国总统唐纳德·特朗普放宽对中国芯片销售的限制，他是保持美国技术流向世界第二大经济体的最直言不讳的倡导者之一。
在美国立法者敦促对中国获取先进计算能力进行更严格控制之际，他的离开可能会削弱华盛顿的这种声音，这可能会增加北京推动半导体自给自足的紧迫性。
中国分析师表示，后果可能是双向的——进一步的限制可能会在短期内限制中国人工智能开发商，同时加强对国内替代品的推动，并为华为等中国芯片制造商创造机会。
黄先生于 11 月 12 日辞职，此前他的婚外情被曝光，其中包括一名被美国官员指控与中国情报机构有联系的中国女性。这标志着他 33 年任期的结束，在此期间，他将 Nvidia 打造成全球领先的人工智能芯片供应商。
他长期以来一直认为，将中国排除在美国芯片技术之外会适得其反，会剥夺美国公司的收入，同时鼓励中国竞争对手开发自己的替代品。
自从黄与一名所谓的中国间谍有牵连的消息传出后，中国外交部一再否认这些间谍指控，称这些指控“毫无根据”，是对中国的“抹黑”。美国官员尚未提供证据证明他们的说法。
在11月12日的例行记者会上，中国外交部发言人毛宁表示，美国“应该停止编造中国间谍故事作为实施技术封锁的借口”，并补充说，中国的技术进步是由自主创新和开放合作驱动的。
中国官方媒体《环球时报》也批评了其所称的对美国科技公司日益增长的政治干预，认为黄的离职反映出越来越多地利用国家安全担忧来限制涉及中国的商业决策。
复旦大学美国研究中心主任吴心伯淡化了这对中国人工智能雄心的潜在影响，他表示，中国已经致力于发展自己的半导体能力，无论华盛顿是否

Would Jensen Huang’s fall dent China’s AI ambitions? | The Straits Times
Would Jensen Huang’s fall dent China’s AI ambitions?
Sign up now: Get insights on Asia's fast-moving developments
Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, seen here addressing media in Beijing in May, is being investigated for being the target of a foreign intelligence operation.
Published Nov 13, 2026, 10:05 PM
Updated Nov 13, 2026, 10:05 PM
Jensen Huang’s resignation at Nvidia has raised fears that the US may tighten chip controls, threatening China’s access to advanced AI computing.
China called the spy claims “purely unsubstantiated” and said the US is using them as a pretext for “technology blockades” against China.
Analysts said pressure on Chinese AI firms may grow in the short term, but the shock could also speed up domestic chip development.
BEIJING – The abrupt resignation of Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang has raised fresh questions about China’s access to advanced American artificial intelligence chips, with Beijing accusing Washington of using espionage allegations to justify tighter technology restrictions even as Chinese analysts play down the potential fallout.
Huang, who personally lobbied US President Donald Trump to ease restrictions on chip sales to China, was among the most vocal advocates for keeping American technology flowing to the world’s second-largest economy.
His departure now threatens to weaken that voice in Washington at a time when US lawmakers are pressing for stricter controls on China’s access to advanced computing power, potentially adding urgency to Beijing’s push for semiconductor self-sufficiency.
Chinese analysts said the consequences could cut both ways – further restrictions may constrain Chinese AI developers in the short term, while strengthening the push for domestic alternatives and creating opportunities for Chinese chipmakers such as Huawei.
Huang’s Nov 12 resignation followed revelations of extramarital affairs, including one involving a Chinese woman alleged by US officials to have links to Chinese intelligence. It marked the end of his 33-year tenure during which he built Nvidia into the world’s leading supplier of the chips that power AI.
He had long argued that excluding China from American chip technology would be counterproductive and would deprive US companies of revenue while encouraging Chinese competitors to develop their own alternatives.
Since news of Huang’s involvement with an alleged Chinese spy broke, China’s Foreign Ministry has repeatedly rejected the espionage allegations, calling them “purely unsubstantiated” and “smears” against China. US officials have not provided evidence for their claims.
At a regular press briefing on Nov 12, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said the US “should stop fabricating the Chinese spy narratives as a pretext for imposing technology blockades,” adding that China’s technological progress is driven by independent innovation and open cooperation.
Chinese state media Global Times also criticised what it described as growing political interference in American technology companies, arguing that Huang’s departure reflected the increasing use of national security concerns to constrain commercial decisions involving China.
Wu Xinbo, director of Fudan University’s Centre for American Studies, played down the potential impact on China’s AI ambitions, saying that China was already committed to developing its own semiconductor capabilities, regardless of whether Washington relaxed or tightened its restrictions.
He pointed to competing views within China over whether to continue purchasing American chips, which still offered performance advantages, or concentrate on developing domestic alternatives.
“If the US tightens its restrictions on chip export controls, which seems likely, it would strengthen the latter camp and benefit Chinese chipmakers,” said Wu, who advises China’s Foreign Ministry.
“The message sent is that the US cannot be relied upon, it can tighten restrictions at any time so we still have to depend on ourselves.”
More fundamentally, Wu said that China and the US were increasingly competing on different fronts. The US is more focused on producing the most advanced AI models, chips and computing capabilities, while Beijing places greater emphasis on commercialising AI and integrating it into manufacturing, healthcare and everyday life.
Zhu Feng, dean of the School of International Studies at Nanjing University, told ST that greater determination to develop domestic alternatives would not immediately close the technological gap.
No impact on chip supply, partnerships amid resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang: Singtel
Why is Nvidia king of the AI chip hill and how soon can rivals catch up?
While tighter restrictions could accelerate investment in domestic alternatives, they would not immediately eliminate China’s dependence on foreign chips, he said. This is because China would not be able to match the capabilities of leading companies such as Nvidia, Taiwan’s TSMC and South Korea’s SK Hynix in the short term, he added.
“Pressure on China will certainly increase in the short term, but in the medium to long term, much depends on whether China can keep its composure and achieve further technological breakthroughs of its own,” he said.
Since 2022, the US government has barred Nvidia from selling its most advanced chips to China. However, in 2025, Trump allowed Nvidia to sell H20 chips to China on a case-by-case basis, and later extended it to Nvidia’s H200 chips.
On Nov 13, shares of Chinese tech companies such as Alibaba, Tencent and Z.ai took a hit as Nvidia’s leadership crisis raised fears that Washington could further tighten restrictions on China’s access to advanced AI computing.
Although Washington restricts direct exports of Nvidia’s top AI chips to China, Chinese companies are still able to rent such advanced computing power from overseas data centres.
In a commentary published on Nov 13 after Huang’s resignation, Global Times warned that other technology executives could face similar scrutiny if their business interests conflicted with Washington’s political agenda.
It also argued that Huang’s Chinese heritage and his calls for continued chip exports had made him particularly vulnerable to political suspicion.

Nanjing University’s Zhu warned that the allegations could fuel a new wave of anti-Chinese sentiment in American political and business circles.
He said the controversy could accelerate efforts by some in Washington to sever technological ties with China, extending beyond chip export controls to broader restrictions on cooperation at a time when advances in AI require both competition and dialogue.
“Whether this will lead to a new Cold War in the field of AI remains to be seen,” he said.
